prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which opened the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred configuration after the full round-1 exchange. The chair asks which criterion should govern when a mature precision measurement meets a younger field-opening discovery. My answer is the one the statutes give: the prize goes to a discovery or invention of importance, and for a physical discovery the test is whether nature surprised us in a way that was then reproduced, not whether every interpretive question has closed. Here a quantitative prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) that a specific twist angle flattens the bands was followed by an experiment (Jarillo-Herrero's group, 2018) that found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle, and the effects have since been reproduced by many groups and in other moire materials. The open pairing mechanism does not undo that, because the citation rests on the existence of flat-band-driven correlated phases and not on a theory of the superconductivity. Mehlig made this point and I agree with him. The round-1 objections are about timing and credit, and I have weighed them, but I do not think they outweigh the case. The theory-pair plus experimental-leader trio is also an unusually direct mapping onto the credited names.
statement.case_against: The maturity objection is held by six colleagues and I cannot wave it away. Eight years is short, the superconducting mechanism and several correlated phases are still debated, and twist-angle disorder limits sample-to-sample reproducibility. The credit objection is the more serious one for me. Yuan Cao, first author of the decisive 2018 papers, is outside the three names, and Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto on the earlier moire theory, and later groups such as Dean, Young and Yazdani, have claims that three places cannot hold. The chair asks how the citation would treat Cao and the earlier theorists. I do not think it can repair the gap. It can only be explicit that it honours the prediction and the discovery in the group that led the experiment, not every contributor, which is what Mehlig proposes. If the committee judges that unrepaired gap too heavy, I would accept B036 as the better-founded prize this year, since its attribution is the cleanest on the list.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct conceptual step, neither the comb nor single-ion control, that allowed many-atom interrogation and the move from 10^-15 to 10^-18, and that maturity is decisive in favour of the clocks this year.
responses.response: This moved me on the overlap question, which was my main objection to B036. I had treated the clock as an application of the frequency comb and of ion control. Her argument that trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength removes the light shift without perturbing the clock transition is a separate idea that neither earlier prize contains, and Kroll and Pearce independently say the same. I now regard B036 as a legitimate discovery-or-invention case and not an extension of 2005 or 2012, and I rank it above B012 as my fallback. I still differ on weighing: she treats an unsettled interpretation as decisive against B022, whereas I think rapid, wide reproduction of a surprising phenomenon is the stronger sign of a lasting result than another digit of precision. That is a difference of criterion, not of fact, and I would not oppose B036 if the committee prefers it. I would ask supporters to keep the citation tied to the lattice concept and to leave Ye's many-body work out, as Olsson suggests, so that it does not read as a second metrology prize.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, puts B036 first and says I underweight the maturity concern and that a prize omitting the person who did the decisive measurement, Cao, invites a credit controversy that the clock prize does not.
responses.response: I accept the asymmetry he names: B036 has the cleaner credit and B022 does not, and I said so in round 1. Where I disagree is that the experimental discovery came from Jarillo-Herrero's group, which led the work Cao carried out, so the laboratory leader is the natural name under the three-person rule, as it is in many earlier prizes. That is a defensible convention, not a hidden injustice. I also note his own reasoning for dropping B017 is exactly this credit problem, so the committee should apply the same standard to both. On maturity, I concede the mechanism is unsettled but would repeat that replication, not mechanism, is what establishes a discovery. I do not agree that waiting a few years is costless, since Bistritzer and MacDonald's prediction is fifteen years old and the committee has no way to know the field will converge on a cleaner story.

responses.point: Mehlig, the only other B022 supporter, says the omission of Cao is the main fairness risk, that the citation should say openly it honours the prediction and discovery and not every contributor, and that B036 is a strong fallback if B022 is judged premature.
responses.response: We agree on essentially everything, including the fallback, and I answer the chair's question for both of us as I understand your position: the citation can name the 2011 prediction and the 2018 discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, and say nothing that implies it settles the pairing mechanism or the full history of the field. I would add one caution to the open-credit wording. A citation cannot say the omission is regrettable, so the committee's own record should show that Cao and the earlier moire theorists were considered. On timing, your argument that the prize rests on flat-band-driven correlated phases and not on a theory of superconductivity is the best answer to the maturity objection, and I rely on it.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B054 as his preferred prize and says that time-reversal-invariant Z2 phases are a different step from the 2016 prize, and that he would take B036 as a serious configuration if the magic-wavelength idea is shown to be decisive.
responses.response: His distinction between a symmetry-protected phase with no broken symmetry and the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz setting is fair, and I withdraw part of my overlap objection to B054. My remaining concern is credit, which he concedes is irreparable: Bernevig, Hughes and the late Zhang made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp's group tested, and the trio omits them. That is a larger gap than for B022, since there the credited names include the prediction of the very angle that the experiment found. His own question about B036 has now been answered by Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce, who all identify the magic-wavelength lattice as the decisive step, and I think that answer is sound.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the comb is only a tool for reading out an optical clock, whereas the new content is the magic-wavelength lattice and the control of systematics, and that the citation should be framed around the lattice concept.
responses.response: I conceded in round 1 that the pending SI redefinition adds no scientific weight, and I note that he and the chair now agree on this too, which makes the case stronger by resting on the measurement and not on a metrology decision. I accept his distinction between the readout tool and the lattice idea. On his Hall-laboratory connection, the chair asks whether it requires recusal. From the record he reports no documented tie to Katori or Ye, and acquaintance through a doctoral lineage alone would not in my view require abstention, but the committee should record it and Kroll should decide for himself in the vote.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the unsettled pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene as a maturity problem; I have not verified the current state of the field beyond what colleagues report.
Whether leaving out Yuan Cao and the earlier moire-theory contributors is acceptable under the three-person limit, or whether the credit gap should lead the committee to prefer B036 this year.

Whether the magic-wavelength lattice is a sufficiently distinct invention to keep B036 clear of the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I now think it is, but I cannot judge priority among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Gill and the national laboratories.
No two-part configuration within three names looks clean. B022 with B036 would need five names, and I see no viable split, so I propose a single part.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My research is in string theory, gravity and cosmology, and none of the shortlisted candidates involves my PhD supervisor David Gross, my mentor Hector Rubinstein, my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet or the Uppsala theory group. My two years at CERN were in the 1990s, before the ATLAS and CMS discovery, and I do not regard that as a recusal issue for B017. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
